pr_title: Netpol: Test that outside world Egress can be effectively allowed while blocking all pod ingress
pr_body:
Follow on to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/91592/ 

**What type of PR is this?**
#96341 Brings up an interesting case wherein we block traffic after allowing everything on 0.0.0.0/0.  Although this is kinda weird as an overall policy, I think its technically valid, and seems to work... although its a little confusing when you read such a policy (normally you'd disallow traffic from the outside and allow on the inside).  I think its a new validation so adding as kind feature.

/kind test

**What this PR does / why we need it**:

Show a clear example of how you can deny internal traffic while allowing external egress traffic in the netpol suite.

**Which issue(s) this PR fixes**: 
Fixes #96341

issue_context.title: Network policies are blocking allowed traffic
issue_context.body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/
-->


**What happened**:
I have set up a network policy that's blocking traffic that it shouldn't
**What you expected to happen**:
Network policies are supposed to block everything that is not allowed. In my case I am allowing egress traffic to everywhere, except the cidr block `192.168.0.0/16`. I can confirm that all traffic to that block is indeed restricted, and mostly anything else is allowed, except for some specific ips (might be affecting the entire `10.0.0.0/8` block as well even though it's not declared as an "except" block, hence should be allowed).

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
1. install eksctl to launch a cluster in EKS (this is where I am testing) (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/eksctl.html)
2. deploy a simple cluster:
```
# test-eksctl.yaml
apiVersion: eksctl.io/v1alpha5
kind: ClusterConfig

metadata:
  name: basic-cluster
  region: us-west-2

nodeGroups:
  - name: ng-1
    instanceType: m5.large
    desiredCapacity: 3
    volumeSize: 80
```
`eksctl create cluster -f test-eksctl.yaml`

3. install calico network plugin:
`kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aws/amazon-vpc-cni-k8s/v1.7.5/config/v1.7/calico.yaml`

4. create a new namespace:
`kubectl create ns netpol-test`

5.  deploy a test pod in this namespace:
```
# netutils.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: netutils-sd1
spec:
  containers:
    - name: my-pod
      image: amouat/network-utils
      command:
      - /bin/sh
      - -c
      - |
        tail -f /dev/null
```
then test basic networking
```
# Deploy the pod
kubectl -n netpol-test apply -f netutils.yaml
 # (This is to grab the cluster ip for the internal kubernetes service, in my case is `10.100.0.1`) 
kubectl get svc -A
# Get a shell in the pod
kubectl -n netpol-test  exec -it  netutils-sd1 bash
# This commands run inside the container
curl -k -I https://10.100.0.1:443
# Which should return 403 forbidden. This is expected, and it purpose is to demonstrate that we can at least hit this ip (we don't care about authentication here, only traffic)
```
6. deploy the following network policy to that namespace:

```
# test-netpol.yaml
kind: NetworkPolicy
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
metadata:
  name: test-netpol
spec:
  egress:
  - to:
    # This should allow communication between pods within this namespace
    - podSelector: {}
    - ipBlock:
        # We need this because we need pods to have connectivity to outside world, but not to pods living in the same cluster in other namespaces
        cidr: 0.0.0.0/0
       # Because all my pods for other namespace will live in the 192.169.0.0/16 block, 
       # I don't want pods from this namespace to reach other namespaces, 
       # this is what I found the easiest way to block connectivity across namespaces.
        except:
        - 192.168.0.0/16
  # This is to allow privileged namespaces like prometheus/kube-system to reach pods in this namespace.
  ingress:
  - from:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 0.0.0.0/0
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
```
`kubectl -n netpol-test apply -f test-netpol.yaml `
Try to hit the ip again:
```
kubectl -n netpol-test  exec -it  netutils-sd1 bash
# This commands run inside the container
curl -k -I https://10.100.0.1:443
# This till it will hang until it times out. This is not expected, as we are not blocking this private ip space anywhere.
```

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`):
```

```
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration: EKS 1.17
- OS (e.g: `cat /etc/os-release`): macos
- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`):

- Network plugin and version (if this is a network-related bug):
* aws-cni
* calico network plugin

@mattfenwick I updated the main ticket with exact steps to reproduce the issue. This should bring up a new empty cluster in AWS and I was able to reproduce it anyway. I am not sure if this problem is within aws / calico / or network policies.
As you can see, I am allowing egress traffic to everywhere `0.0.0.0/0` except `192.168.0.0/16`. Egress to `10.100.0.1` should be then allowed, but it's not (you can tell because before applying the network policy, the traffic is allowed, and after the network policy is deployed, the traffic is restricted)

@scardena there might be a better way to write your network policies -- there are a couple problems with the policy and its comments don't match the code, I suggest instead:

 - [use this](https://github.com/ahmetb/kubernetes-network-policy-recipes/blob/master/04-deny-traffic-from-other-namespaces.md) to block traffic from other namespaces while allowing traffic within a namespace

 - to allow traffic from a specific namespace (`# This is to allow privileged namespaces like prometheus/kube-system to reach pods in this namespace.`) follow [this example using namespace labels](https://github.com/ahmetb/kubernetes-network-policy-recipes/blob/master/06-allow-traffic-from-a-namespace.md)

 - to allow traffic to the outside world, check out [this example](https://github.com/ahmetb/kubernetes-network-policy-recipes/blob/master/08-allow-external-traffic.md)

One big advantage of using these examples is they don't make assumptions about CIDR ranges, so they're much easier to manage!

I tried out the example on my KinD/Calico cluster and wasn't able to repro the behavior you saw.  [Here's what I used](https://gist.github.com/mattfenwick/4a05cc0a2f953045f70cb75e48691906).

Just speculating here -- is your cluster ipv4, ipv6, or dual stack?  Also wondering if the netpol itself might be the problem: the netpol has both a podselector and and ipblock for one of the egress rules, but [according to the docs](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ef16faf409b7aec6b2171ec3e4a39c3f3f68c030/pkg/apis/networking/types.go#L181-L182), this isn't allowed -- no idea what effect this would have (maybe kube should do some validation there and report that as a problem instead of accepting malformed input?)

I think the best bet is to rework your network policy using the above examples -- CIDRs don't seem like a good match for your use case, I think the namespace labels and selectors will be a better fit!

@mattfenwick the reason we are using cidr blocks, is because in AWS we need the pods to get ingress traffic from the AWS ALB provisioned by the AWS Ingress Controller (If we were using nginx as ingress controller, it would be easy, we just select the nginx pods for ingress traffic to our pods). so our conclusion was that the best way to block traffic between namespaces was:
1. allow ingress traffic from everywhere for a given namespace (this allows the pods to get traffic from the AWS load balancer, and allow ingress traffic from prometheus/fluentd namespaces)
2. allow all egress traffic except to the private space `192.168.0.0/16`, which basically restricts pods from namespace A to reach pods in namespace B,C,D...and so on (all our pods in live in `192.168.0.0/16`). A main requirement is that the pods need to have access to the outside world, that's why we are opening egress to everywhere, except for the private space where all the other pods live.
